On 12/01/2017 09:01 AM, Chester Kam wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> I have recently read the latest article by Devlieger and Rosseel in the
> journal Methodology, and it is an excellent article that discsused the
> use of Croon's approach to conduct factor score path analysis. At the
> end of the article, however, Devlieger and Rosseel states:
>
> 'For the moment, the method of Croon also does not work for connected
> measurement models, such as models with cross-loadings or correlated
> residual errors.'
>
> I am curious why the approach is inappropriate for models with
> cross-loadings? Any reference will be helpful!

The original idea was to create factor scores for each latent variable,
*one at a time*. Once the factor scores are computed, we apply Croon's
correction, followed by a path analysis using these factor scores as if
they were observed.

Of course, if you have cross-loadings, or correlated residuals across
latent variables, they will be ignored in this approach. One way out is
to extend the measurement model to include all 'connected' items, and
compute the factor scores for all latent variables involved
simultaneously. The best way to handle this is still under study.

Yves.

No no. The first latent mean is 'fixed to zero', but the second one is

significant.

Given that lavInspect() can return R^2:

?lavInspect

The example from the ?bootstrapLavaan help page can be easily adapted:

R2.orig <- fitMeasures(fitmymodel, "rsquare")
## get a bootstrap distribution
R2.boot <- bootstrapLavaan(fitmymodel, R=1000,
                           FUN = lavInspect, what = "rsquare")
## calculate percentile 95% CIs
apply(R2.boot, 2, quantile, probs = c(.025, .975))

Note that a CI is a range of null-hypothesized parameter values that would not be rejected by the data, given the alpha level (1 - confidence level).

The cor2cov() function is meant for when you already have a full correlation matrix rather than a lower/upper triangle; it was not meant to be a required second step.

> It also appears that when using "inspect(modelname, what = "sampstat")" in their model, that a covariance matrix is created, but this matrix is different than one created manually by the students. Not sure what Lavaan is pulling on the back end.

SEM is based on asymptotic theory, so when maximum (normal) likelihood estimation is used, it rescales the covariance matrix so that the sums of squares and cross-products are divided by N (population formula) rather than N - 1 (sample estimator of population value).  So the "sampstat" output should be your sample.cov= input times (N - 1)/N.

> My question: does Lavaan know that a correlation matrix needs to become a covariance matrix and creates one automatically? Or, does it treat it as a covariance matrix without any transformation?

It took me a while to find out what you were talking about, because you posted gigantic RMarkdown files instead of posting a small, minimally sufficient example to reproduce your problem.  It would be helpful if you did so in the future, to save volunteers time when providing help.

lavaan() does not have an argument sds= for you to pass SDs for scaling a correlation matrix.  The argument sample.cov= expects just that: a sample covariance matrix.

?lavOptions

So you/they need to use the getCov() OR cor2cov() function to create the sample covariance matrix, then pass that to lavaan().

Diya,
Don't tweak, supplement.

lavInspect(fit2, what='cov.lv <http://cov.lv>')

On Saturday, December 2, 2017 at 3:00:06 PM UTC-8, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > When they use the getcov function + the cor2cov to transform their data from a correlation matrix to a covariance matrix
>
> Why would they need both functions?  getCov() already includes an sds= argument, so you can include them in the getCov() function when you pass the lower triangle of correlations.  The cor2cov() function is meant for when you already have a full correlation matrix rather than a lower/upper triangle; it was not meant to be a required second step.
>
> > It also appears that when using "inspect(modelname, what = "sampstat")" in their model, that a covariance matrix is created, but this matrix is different than one created manually by the students. Not sure what Lavaan is pulling on the back end.
>
> SEM is based on asymptotic theory, so when maximum (normal) likelihood estimation is used, it rescales the covariance matrix so that the sums of squares and cross-products are divided by N (population formula) rather than N - 1 (sample estimator of population value).  So the "sampstat" output should be your sample.cov= input times (N - 1)/N.
>
> > My question: does Lavaan know that a correlation matrix needs to become a covariance matrix and creates one automatically? Or, does it treat it as a covariance matrix without any transformation?
>
> It took me a while to find out what you were talking about, because you posted gigantic RMarkdown files instead of posting a small, minimally sufficient example to reproduce your problem.  It would be helpful if you did so in the future, to save volunteers time when providing help.
>
> lavaan() does not have an argument sds= for you to pass SDs for scaling a correlation matrix.  The argument sample.cov= expects just that: a sample covariance matrix.
>
> ?lavOptions
>
> So you/they need to use the getCov() OR cor2cov() function to create the sample covariance matrix, then pass that to lavaan().

> if I understand correctly, all "robust" methods in lavaan relate to a robust estimation of the standard error and/or test statistics, but not to a robust estimation of the parameters themselves.

That is certainly true for all the MLM, MLMV, MLR estimators. But estimator 'WLS' (also known as ADF) is different: this one may end up with different estimates that are (in very large samples only) 'robust' against distributional misspecification. But they are not 'outlier-robust'.

>
> There are a lot of regression techniques that provide robust estimation of the parameter (e.g., robust against outliers), such as Theil-Sen estimators or M-estimators.
>
> Is anybody aware of such robust methods in SEM? (In particular: estimators with a high breakdwon point that are robust against outliers).

See package 'rsem'. This builds on work done by Kei-Hai Yuan (and Peter Bentler) two decades ago. See:

Yuan, K. H., & Bentler, P. M. (1998). Robust mean and covariance structure analysis. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 51(1), 63-88.

Including all of this in lavaan has been on my TODO list for a long time...

Yves.

Michelle,
Two things stand out for me.

First, your expression for the covariance matrix appears incomplete, missing a right bracket and right parenthesis.  However, that is the the reason for the error.

Second, a lavaan model syntax string provides model syntax for a single model.  You cannot include distinct models within the same model syntax string.  For example, the following two specifications specify the same model.

'Stooges ~ Larry + Curly + Moe'

'Stooges ~ Larry
Stooges ~ Curly
Stooges ~ Moe'

In both cases, there is just one equation for Stooges that predicts Stooges from Larry, Curly and Moe.

Syntax such as the following is not valid.

'Stooges ~ Larry + Curly
Stooges ~ Larry + Moe'

When the model syntax interpreter reaches the second Larry, it recognizes this as a duplicate of the first.  You cannot list Stooges ~ Larry twice in the same parameter table as two distinct parameters.  So, one of the Larrys has to be omitted in order to make the above syntax valid.

You have listed the same variable several times in your various lines beginning 'total_anxiety ~'.  That is the reason for the error.

Maybe you can adapt lavaan's lav_matrix_duplication_ginv_pre_post()
function,  which usually expects a S %x% S matrix as the argument (and
therefore insists that the number of rows/cols is some number (n =
nrow(S)) squared. The current code is:

# pre AND post-multiply with D^+: D^+ %*% A %*% t(D^+)
# for square matrices only, with ncol = nrow = n^2
lav_matrix_duplication_ginv_pre_post <- function(A = matrix(0,0,0)) {

     A <- as.matrix(A)

     # number of columns
     n2 <- NCOL(A)

     # square A only, n2 = n^2
     stopifnot(NROW(A) == n2, sqrt(n2) == round(sqrt(n2)))

     # dimension
     n <- sqrt(n2)

     idx1 <- lav_matrix_vech_idx(n); idx2 <- lav_matrix_vechru_idx(n)
     OUT <- (A[idx1,,drop=FALSE] + A[idx2,,drop=FALSE]) / 2
     OUT <- (OUT[,idx1,drop=FALSE] + OUT[,idx2,drop=FALSE]) / 2
     OUT
}

This would avoid creating the Dplus matrix, which can be huge (and is
very sparse).

Another option is to use the Matrix package, and define Dplus as a
sparse matrix.

The critical thing is to start with a '>' prompt before you execute the script.  Under no circumstances should you encounter a double '+' prompt. messages.body_plain:
> I'm also looking for a way to find how much variance in my DVs (latents) is explained by my IVs (predictors).
>
> I've tried inspect(fit, 'r2') but that only gives me the variance explained by each of my latent variables.

Are you sure you have latent DVs in your model?  That syntax will return R-squared for all outcomes, both latent and observed.  Behold:

library(lavaan)
example(sem)
inspect(fit, 'r2')

   x1    x2    x3    y1    y2    y3    y4    y5    y6    y7    y8 dem60 dem65
0.846 0.947 0.761 0.723 0.475 0.574 0.702 0.667 0.570 0.643 0.687 0.200 0.965

> How can I find out how much variance is explained by each predictor?

That is not available, only the variance explained by all predictors of an outcome.  Decomposing R-squared into components due to separate factors is only possible when the predictors have correlations == 0 (e.g., orthogonal designs / balanced groups in ANOVA).  If predictors are correlated, then they share some credit for explaining variance, so there is no R-squared per predictor.  There is the concept of partial-eta-squared, which is the proportional reduction in residual variance after adding an effect, but that is not provided by lavaan.  You would have to run a model with and without an effect to calculate how much the residual variance decreases, and divide that by the larger residual variance to express it as a proportion (i.e., partial-eta-squared).

On Thursday, 14 December 2017 11:35:29 UTC, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I'm also looking for a way to find how much variance in my DVs (latents) is explained by my IVs (predictors).
> >
> > I've tried inspect(fit, 'r2') but that only gives me the variance explained by each of my latent variables.
>
> Are you sure you have latent DVs in your model?  That syntax will return R-squared for all outcomes, both latent and observed.  Behold:
>
> library(lavaan)
> example(sem)
> inspect(fit, 'r2')
>
>    x1    x2    x3    y1    y2    y3    y4    y5    y6    y7    y8 dem60 dem65
> 0.846 0.947 0.761 0.723 0.475 0.574 0.702 0.667 0.570 0.643 0.687 0.200 0.965
>
> > How can I find out how much variance is explained by each predictor?
>
> That is not available, only the variance explained by all predictors of an outcome.  Decomposing R-squared into components due to separate factors is only possible when the predictors have correlations == 0 (e.g., orthogonal designs / balanced groups in ANOVA).  If predictors are correlated, then they share some credit for explaining variance, so there is no R-squared per predictor.  There is the concept of partial-eta-squared, which is the proportional reduction in residual variance after adding an effect, but that is not provided by lavaan.  You would have to run a model with and without an effect to calculate how much the residual variance decreases, and divide that by the larger residual variance to express it as a proportion (i.e., partial-eta-squared).

> what should I do for the syntax?

Since you posted your model syntax in another thread, I'll follow-up here.  I label your parameters using "b" for beta (regression slopes) and "p" for psi (covariance matrix of disturbances).  It helps if you can find a text explaining covariance algebra and/or path-tracing rules, like Loelin's (2004) Latent Variable Models (4th ed.) or Bollen's (1989) Structural Equations with Latent Variables.  You can ask around on SEMNET for resources to learn path-tracing rules and covariance algebra.

Model <- '
## slopes
m_envy ~ b21*unfair
cb ~ b32*m_envy

## (residual) variances
unfair ~~ p11*unfair
m_envy ~~ p22*m_envy
cb  ~~ p33*cb

######## model constraints:

## exogengous predictor, constrain variance to 1
p11 == 1

## residual variance is a function of variance explained by "unfair"
p22 == 1 - b21*p11*b21

## residual variance is a function of variance explained by "m_envy", some of which is explained by "unfair"
p33 == 1 - b32*p22*b32 - b32*b21*p11*b21*b32

'

If you also fit a partial-mediation model, where unfair also has a direct effect on cb (e.g., labeled "b31"), then you need to take into account both sources of explained variance (i.e., also subtract b31*p11*b31).

> 1) given the skew and non-normality of the item distributions, and different item types, I chose WLSMV which has considerably better fit than MLR, is this appropriate?

They are just as (un)informative with DWLS as ML estimation, but don't take suggested cutoffs too seriously:

http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1094428110368562

You seem to consider probability, magnitude, and duration to be 3 separate constructs, but intuitively it seems the general factor is negative perception, measured by 22 events from a population of events/items you could have asked them about, and probability, magnitude, and duration are the method factors for assessing how negative something is.

messages.body_plain:
> The summary of fit measures provides me with two different chi-square values for the two samples

No, those are each group's contribution to the chi-squared statistic.  If you made no equality constraints across groups (configural invariance), then those contributions would be equivalent to the individual chi-squared statistics from separate 1-group models fit to each sample.  But when you have equality constraints across groups, that will not be the case: each group has some influence over parameters that apply to them both, so the chi-squared contributions (and associated degrees of freedom) are not independent.

> what do supplemental fit measures in the output refer to?

Overall (mis)fit of the model to both groups, simultaneously.

> Is there a way to get either an individual chi-square value for the whole sample

Yes, that is the line at the top of the summary() output, labeled "Model Fit Test Statistic" (with its df and p value below it).

> or supplemental fit indices by group?

No, not when there are constraints across groups, because you cannot simply divide the df in half between the groups.  (Some df were obtained by constraining loadings across groups.)

> In testing for strong measurement invariance (equal factor loadings and thresholds), the delta/CFI was lower than the recommend threshold (see Cheung & Rensvold, 2000).

That threshold is invalid:

http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10705511.2014.882658

> When I used the MODINDICES command, there are no threshhold modification indices. How can I see which item do I have to release?

Because you are already estimating all of your thresholds.  The modindices() function only returns indices for parameters that are fixed to a certain value (e.g., zero). HSMiss <- HolzingerSwineford1939[ , c(paste("x", 1:9, sep = ""),

textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6

               miArgs = list(noms = "school"))

               miArgs = list(noms = "school"), estimator = "mlm")

You have freed the first oading on the common factor, but not otherwise scaled the factor. So my guess would be that lavaan is implicitly constrfaining another loading to achieve identification. If you add a line to scale the factor, like:
MAPG~~1*MAPG
that may resolve the warning message.

I am by intent not addressing the problem of factor indeterminacy.

Hi Terrence,

Something is still not right.  I am running SemTools version 0.4-15.tar.gz, lavaan version .6-1.1183, and R version 3.43.  I get the following error messages when I run the code below
There were 20 warnings (use warnings() to see them)
> anova(fitmi, indices=TRUE)
Error in anova(fitmi, indices = TRUE) :
  trying to get slot "imputed" from an object of a basic class ("logical") with no slots
> summary(fitmi)
** WARNING ** lavaan (0.6-1.1183) model has NOT been fitted

** WARNING ** Estimates below are simply the starting values

The 20 warnings are all the same and say
1: In if (class(model) == "formula") { ... :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used

I appreciate your patience, but I am planning to cover multiple imputation via lavaan and semTools in my upcoming SEM course.

David

-----------
require(semTools)
require(lavaan)
require(mice)

scimodel <- read.csv(file.choose(),header=T)

## Generate some missing values ####
scimodel$ses[scimodel$ses >=.9] <- NA
scimodel$sciach[scimodel$sciach >=30.00] <- NA
scimodel$scigrade6[scimodel$scigrade6 == 1] <- NA

## Science Achievement Example
## Kaplan (2009, pg. 15)
pathmodel <- '

# regressions
sciach ~ scigrade10
scigrade10 ~ scigrade6+ses+certsci+understand+challenge
challenge~understand
understand ~ certsci

'

### Multiple imputation using MICE ###

scimodel_imp<-mice(scimodel, m = 5, method="pmm")
mice.imp <- NULL
for(i in 1:5) mice.imp[[i]] <- complete(scimodel_imp, action=i, inc=FALSE)

# run lavaan with previously imputed data using runMI
# Note that MLR handles the non-normality

fitmi <- runMI(pathmodel,estimator="ml",
               data=mice.imp,
               fun="sem")
anova(fitmi, indices=TRUE)   # Fit statistics are not provided with the 'anova' command #
summary(fitmi)
-------------
